text: Lesson 17 told you what belongs in a portfolio repo: the SSIS package, the T-SQL DDL, the SSRS report definition, screenshots, and a README. This lesson is where you actually build that repo, using the Git fundamentals from How IT Teams Work, Lesson 5 — so if you haven't taken that lesson yet, go do it first.

Turning your local capstone folder into a pushed GitHub repo takes five commands. First, git init starts tracking the folder, git add stages everything, and git commit saves that first snapshot. Then, after creating an empty repository on GitHub with no README or .gitignore added there, git remote add origin points your local repo at it, git branch dash M main names your branch, and git push dash u origin main sends your commits up. From here on, every change is the same three-step loop: add, commit, push.

Not everything in your local folder belongs in the repo. A .gitignore file, written before your first commit, should list local SSMS or Visual Studio settings files, any connection string or credentials file you created for local testing, and large exported data files you used along the way. Lesson 5 covered why this matters: once something is committed, it's recoverable from history forever, even after a later commit deletes it.

A repo that exists isn't the same as a repo that works as evidence. Check it the way a reviewer would. Can a stranger, signed out of GitHub, read your dtsx and SQL files directly, with no download required? Does the README explain the business problem before it lists any files? Are the SSRS and Power BI screenshots actually visible, not just linked? And does the commit history show more than one commit, so it reads as a real project, not a single file dump?

If any of that is a no, that's a real gap to fix, not a detail to skip. Next lesson, you'll look at the questions a Microsoft BI developer candidate actually gets asked, so you know exactly what to prepare for.
